utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin, as usual I'm addressing you, hoping to hear the same reply. Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. And General Talic, good morning to you. Same question are you hearing me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman and I appear with Milka Maglov and Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, and appearances for General Talic? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Xavier de Roux, attorney, assisted by Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic and Fabien Masson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. So is there anything you want to raise before we start with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I've handed to the registry, representative of the Registry, the sitting list. I agree more or less with what Mr. Ackerman and Mr. de Roux have suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's perfect. I thank you. So I think we can admit the witness. Yes, please call the case. It's an oversight of mine. In case we don't know that we are sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly, before I forget it the order that was issued yesterday with regard to humanitarian organisations has, as part of it, that if an ex parte application is to be made in accordance with that order by the Defence, that the organisation should also receive notification. There is no indication in the order as to how that notification should be done. I don't know how to do that. And so some way -- the Defence should be provided with a manner in which to notify the organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll have a look at it again. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can assist to this extent: We can provide to Your Honour and to the Defence the name of the person who we have been dealing with which may assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we need a fax number or something. There must be something beyond the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Ms. Korner. Thank you. All right, thank you Mr. Ackerman. Thank you Ms. Korner

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just before the witness comes in, on that note we propose today to disclose to the Defence the two statements that are involved at present. And we would hope to call the witnesses immediately after the Easter break, subject to their convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Dzonlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Dzonlic. Again, once more, may I ask you to read the statement that you read yesterday and the day before? Then you may sit down and you will be questioned further by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You my sit down. Ms. Korner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I wonder if the witness could be handed again the documents or the set of documents he was looking at yesterday, which bear the exhibit number, P227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had arrived at decision number 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, could you go to item number 13, please, on that decision number 4? It's the last item.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that show that professor Dragolub Mirjanic is hereby appointed a new member of the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, replacing Rajko Kuzmanovic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it says, but instead of Rajko Kuzmanovic, it says Dragolub Mirjanic. I heard a different name. Any way it's Dragolub Mirjanic. Just in the way it says here in the document. Maybe the interpretation was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've only drawn attention to that because it explains the decision -- well, what's happened I feel is -- can I for a moment digress and show Your Honours? Your Honours, I think I referred to in it in opening but there is a different version of this document which is disclosure number 313 in the binders. It's Exhibit -- sorry, just a moment -- P168, and the original B/C/S version, which is on the back, shows a couple of handwritten names at the end, but that shows Dr. Kuzmanovic. The gazette, of course was published considerably after. This is clearly an original published at the time so obviously the gazette by that stage replaced the names. We think what's happened is that, not surprisingly, a lot of cutting and pasting goes on to save time and the translation must have cut and paste from the original document, but as I say, it is being corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it does seem--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does seem, nonetheless, that initially, at least on -- as a result of the meeting or during the meeting of the 5th May, it was Dr. Rajko Kuzmanovic that was appointed as one of the members of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Now, assuming that Crisis Staff and war -- and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is one and the same thing, it seems to me that something must have happened between the 5th and the 8th of May, presumably either the non-acceptance on the part of Kuzmanovic or anything might have happened. And he was replaced by Professor Dragolub Mirjanic during the meeting of the 8th of May. This is how I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So but in any case, it does seem to me also that an explanation was needed because the B/C/S translation or version of what appears to be decision number 2 shows directly Mirjanic and not Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So is the picture clear to everyone now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. It's not even close to clear. There are just a myriad of problems with this, Your Honour, and I don't know when, if ever, they will get resolved, but these documents are not the same. There are multiple documents appointing -- purporting to appoint members of this Crisis Staff, War Presidency, whatever it's called, and they are all different. And I think at some point the Prosecution sort of needs to decide which of these documents they are going to argue to you is the authentic document. But one of the documents appoints an entirely different Crisis Staff than others. And I don't know that the Prosecution is even capable of proving which one is authoritative. Ordinarily one would say that published in the Official Gazette is the authoritative document but it's obviously not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What still remain unanswered to an extent, I mean, what -- I mean this is not something which is going to throw the case one way or another in any case, but what we have here definitely, I mean also so that you know beforehand how my mind works at least, that to me, what should be looked at by the Trial Chamber as the most reliable or the original document that we have is the official government -- Official Gazette or government gazette, et cetera. If what is purported to be a translation contains something which does not tally with the original Official Gazette, then obviously what would be required is an explanation. And the explanation that is forthcoming from the Prosecution is that there might have been some cutting and pasting which resulted in someone including in the name -- in the list the alteration, the change or the new-comer in the sort of a pre-emptive manner. Which again -- I mean, may be accepted and it's not going to change much. Yes, have you finished, Mr. Ackerman? Because there is also Maitre de Roux behind you and his figure is more imposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I finish the train of thought that I'm on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The problem, Your Honour, is this. The -- what is published in the Official Gazette, which one ordinarily would think is the authoritative version flies in the face of all the evidence. There is a document that Ms. Korner referred to, and I think it has a Prosecution number, which has in that list of persons, it has a number 16 and a number 17, and those have been translated - and, Ms. Korner, I'm looking at your document 2.10 at this point - been translated as the 15 named members plus the presidents of the War Presidencies of the municipalities and the deputies of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also as members of the Crisis Staff. And I believe that the evidence in the case will show that that was in fact the makeup of the Crisis Staff and not what appears in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Maitre de Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to make a very simple remark, and that is that this cannot be a problem of translation because it is quite clear, I have before my eyes the original of the Official Gazette, and the Official Gazette does not mention the name of Mr. Kuzmanovic. Therefore, what is presented as a translation of the decision cannot be a translation of the decision. This is a document which was compiled, I don't know how, but it cannot be translation, because a translation cannot replace one name by another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, you are right, but what -- there is definitely a problem of translation as regards document 2, because document 2, in the original, what is purported to be the original Official Gazette, as you correctly state, number 11, member number 11, in the Crisis Staff, is Dragolub Mirjanic and not Kuzmanovic. So presumably one would not have expected that to be translated into Kuzmanovic. That's what -- that's why I actually stated earlier that some sort of explanation ought to be forthcoming. On the other hand, it is also, and it should be also obvious -- if it's obvious to me, it should be obvious to you, that if that is the case, if in other words on the 5th of May of 1992, the composition agreed upon or established was as shown in the government gazette here. In other words, member number 11 was Dragolub Mirjanic. Then I don't see any sense at all, when in the next page, number 13, you have exactly the B/C/S version of what you find in the English translation. In other words, it says - I don't know the language, but I can -- I know a little bit of Cyrillic so I can understand what it states, and basically it states that Kuzmanovic is being replaced by Dragolub Mirjanic. So if an explanation is in order from the Prosecution, the Prosecution can actually rely on the discrepancy that emerges from the original document itself, even though this makes confusion more confounded to an extent but more or less, I mean, I think the Trial Chamber is happy with the explanation given that it may have been a case of cutting and pasting and within three days the picture changed somehow and one person replaced another and whoever was in charge of issuing or publishing the government gazette may have had a document with some note on it or something, as normally happens sometimes. Yes, Ms. Korner? Sorry to have kept you standing for so long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say I'm only guessing this is what the Translation Department did. It's nothing to do with the Prosecution or whatever and it's not a confusion about the document. I don't know what document Mr. Ackerman has referred to, because 2.10, according to our records, is addressed to all municipal boards of the SDS to assess the possibility of establishing a Serbian municipality. Our case is that there was a change in the composition of the Crisis Staff/War Staff/War Presidency, which replaced Dr. Rajko Kuzmanovic with the other gentleman and there was also a change in the last two, from the -- that original handwritten to what went into the gazette. And I don't know what Mr. Ackerman is talking about because those are the only documents that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 3.13, I read the wrong number. There are two translations that I've been provided of that document, of that same document. They are slightly different translations of that document. But they are both obviously translations of 3.13.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Your Honour have a copy of it there? If not -- I'm going to ask for it to be put up on the ELMO and then Your Honours can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes. 313.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P168, binder 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P168 and I would like to see it in both verses, English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are two English versions which as long as we are putting them on the ELMO both the English versions need to go on too, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, could I ask the usher when he has a moment to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. give me the two English versions that Mr. Ackerman is talking about? Because we are only aware of one. Your Honour, I'm sorry this is taking time and I'm sorry, Mr. Dzonlic because I think it's worth sorting out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so because I figure out this might happen again and again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: One appears to be a translation done by yourself, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are both I got from you. I haven't done translations myself. I think one of them may have been an attachment, early on an attachment, supporting document. It may have come out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm helpfully told by Ms. Gustin one is a draft translation. In the good old days we got a draft done into final and so the other is the final translation. Your Honour, can I ask that the -- first of all the English version be put up on the ELMO? And can we go down to the bottom of the document, please? And perhaps you could put it in the middle somewhere? Thank you. Right. Your Honour will see that number 16 and 17, presidents of RP municipalities or number 16, presidents of RP municipalities and then something illegible in handwriting is number 17. If we turn it over so that the B/C/S version is there, Your Honours will see that the two handwritten ones, and what appears to be the stamp and signature of Mr. Erceg. So this was -- it would appear from the face of it -- to be the document that was produced at or about the time, before it got into the gazette. Now, if one goes back to the document that we are looking -- that we were looking at with the witness -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Korner. The microphone has been switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I could have that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've not seen the other English translation which I think you have to see. I ask that it be put on the ELMO and it hasn't yet. It should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The draft or the final?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says draft but it seems to be more accurate than what says final because it includes the language from paragraphs 16 and 17 where the other one leaves it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we no longer -- I no longer have the draft. Perhaps Mr. Ackerman would like it put it on the ELMO. Arrange for it to be put on the ELMO. I think, Your Honour, what -- I'm guessing and we can get whoever translated it to say, is that's what the original translator thought was written. Whoever revised it for the final decided that it was not clear enough and that's why it's left out but that's a guess. Your Honour, in any event, that's apparently that. But if one goes back to the gazette which we are looking at, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's fairly clear what happened now. It's even -- before it was a little bit nebulous but now it's very clear. What obviously happened was that on the 5th of May or thereabouts, there was this document forthcoming from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Executive council, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, which had, on the face of it, two blanks to be filled in, in other words, the insertion of two specific names. One would be number 17, being the presidents of the municipalities, and the other one, whoever you said. And number 11, in the meantime, was definitely at the time, Mr. Kuzmanovic. What happened is that on the 8th a decision was taken to replace Kuzmanovic with Dragolub Mirjanic and in the meantime, the two names that would have featured or been slotted in number 16 and number 17, were known. So whoever was responsible for the publication took the liberty of filling in number 16 and 17 with the names of the two persons indicated to him. In the meantime he must have or she must have known that Kuzmanovic had been replaced by Mirjanic and there you are. You have someone affecting the changes maybe with or without authority, but that explains what could have possibly and, not just possibly, very possibly happen. Yes, Mr. Ackerman? I think we are wasting time actually, but I am, of course, I'm very anxious to hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- all these documents I was intending to use during my cross-examination, but now that the matter has come up it would almost look disingenuous if I wait and do it then rather than make it clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's only fair that you do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is another document called 3.450 from the Prosecution which also purports -- which I have marked as defendant Brdjanin Exhibit 49A and B, and the English translation is not a draft translation. It's a final translation. And it lists as a member of the Crisis Staff someone named Milan Cuvalic [phoen] in the translated version, in the B/C/S version, that person is listed as Milan Puvacic, which is a completely different name and could not possibly have been mistranslated. And so the mystery deepens how these things happen. Ms. Korner takes the position that that one document that we just looked at was a draft translation so it must not be right but here is a final translation that has the same kind of errors in it. And I'm not sure it's possible for the Prosecution to establish who was on this Crisis Staff at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner? Let's not waste much more time on this. Mr. Ackerman must remember also that there may be very often the most simple explanation for all these. My name in Malta has been published. Sometimes they transpose the I with the U and I become a different person or sometimes people who know me by my real name, Carmel and others know me by my other name Lino so it goes all -- and I become Carmel Lino Agius, Carmen A. Agius and there is a hell of a lot of confusion. And it's all the same person, I can assure you. No schizophrenia involved. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I agree with you. I don't think we need to pursue this digression any further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I'm sorry for that. Could I just ask you then finally on this topic, do you know first of all who Dr. Rajko Kuzmanovic was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know who Professor Rajko Kuzmanovic was. He was my professor at the law school in Banja Luka. He taught me political science, about political systems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the gentleman who replaced him, Mirjanic, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he is, but I have heard about Dr. Dragolub Mirjanic but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Can we now move on to a further conclusion in the gazette? If we could go, please, to number 6? Yes, number 6, please. And if we look at conclusion number 2, the item that starts, "Decisions adopted by the War Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to be strictly respected in all public and economic organisations." Now, you've already told us that the majority of companies in the Banja Luka area at this stage were state-owned. How would such a conclusion or such a decision be enforced?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, this conclusion that I have, it is on page 6, in the second part. The session of the 9th of May, 1992, of the Crisis Staff, paragraph 2 of the conclusion, item 2 of the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you -- I'm sorry, in case you haven't found it, I'm asking you about the decision, the part of paragraph number 2, which is the last part, in the English translation, "Decisions adopted by the War Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to be strictly respected in all public and economic organisations."

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the question was: How would such a decision -- in other words, that decisions made by the War Crisis Staff are to be strictly respected --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't say War Crisis Staff, it says War Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite. Some objections perhaps are more pertinent than others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "By the War Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina are to be strictly respected." How would such a decision be enforced?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff adopted decisions and conclusions and issued orders to economic agents and determined the process of work, the manner of operating for each economic organisation. An economic organisation had to provide a war plan of work, so to speak, and only after this had been authorised by the Crisis Staff, in such a case the organisation was able to continue with its operations. This meant reducing the number of those employed, and directing production towards wartime objectives. When an economic organisation was given the green light, the go ahead, for the wartime plan for the process of production, then it was possible to appoint, to management places and positions, only citizens of Serbian nationality who were loyal to the Serbian Republic, as they called it in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they had to confirm that they were loyal by responding to the mobilisation from 1991, which had been issued during the war in Croatia. On that basis, and on the basis of these loyal people and those who had been assigned to positions of responsibility, on this basis, it was possible to implement the decisions of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as the work plans were concerned, you've said that it was possible to appoint to management positions -- places and positions, only citizens of Serbian nationality. What happened to those who were of non-Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be dismissed from their jobs. They -- their employment was terminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph, the same paragraph, number 2, also refers to "Only persons loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may make decisions on the implementation of the general mobilisation in public and economic organisations." What would happen to Serb employees of companies who were liable to be mobilised? And before you answer that question, I should ask you so that we get it clear, between what ages were people -- were men liable for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conscripts were all adults, up 60 years of age, I think. And an adult according to our law is someone who is between the age of 18 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if a Serb employee of a company was liable to mobilisation, what would or could happen?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the wartime plan of a certain economic organisation had been authorised, if it had been given the go-ahead for the process of production, and if it -- if this authorisation had been given by the Crisis Staff, if such an employee or citizen of Serbian nationality was necessary for the process of production in that organisation, he would then be given a wartime assignment at his work and that would be his mobilisation position. This was called a work duty. And if he was not necessary for the process of production, he would be mobilised and given a wartime assignment, I assume, at the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were non-Serb employees of the companies ever given this wartime assignment at what was his place of work?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people, usually professionals for certain posts, and they were of non-Serb nationality, and because of the process of production, an assignment was authorised for them. That is to say, work obligations were assigned to them, up until the moment when -- up until such time as a Serbian person would appear and who was as qualified as he was, and in such cases, he would replace him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next, can I ask you to move, please, to conclusion number 7 or I suppose item number 7, the 11th of May, 1992 document? The first item on that conclusion refers to the "surrender of illegally acquired weapons" and extends the deadline to the 14th of May, from the original deadline, which -- I can't find now the part where -- but it says, "This deadline expired today, the 11th of May, and has been extended at the request of citizens of all nationalities. This decision was explained by the wish of -- for the weapons to be returned in a peaceful manner and without police intervention. After the deadline expires, weapons will be confiscated by employees of the Security Services Centre of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and severe sanctions will be imposed on those who ignore the call of the Crisis Staff." In your capacity on the executive board of the SDA, were you aware of any request made for an extension of the deadline?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware of the fact that the deadline for the surrender of weapons had been extended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is did anyone on the Bosniak -- of the Bosniak representatives ask for an extension of a deadline, that you're aware of, obviously?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of the Bosniaks at any time asked for the deadline for the surrender of weapons to be extended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 5 on that same conclusion, in number 7, says, "All work plans of Krajina enterprises must be analysed and approved by the National Defence Council of the relevant municipality or by the War Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Is that what you referred to in your previous answer about the work plans that companies had to produce?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was thinking about, referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, on this one, item number 6, "All able-bodied men aged between 18 and 55 years, who have fled from the Autonomous Region of Krajina must immediately return to their municipalities and help their fellow citizens in the fight against the enemy. Ignoring the above-mentioned calls shall result in a ban on the return of the said individuals to their homes, that is, to the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and the confiscation of all their property, both moveable and immovable." Mr. Dzonlic, what effect did that decision have on non-Serbs living in Banja Luka? Or who were no longer living in Banja Luka, I should say, who had left? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The non-Serbs who had left Banja Luka did not know of this decision because they were not in Banja Luka, but this decision in a most drastic way violated the basic human rights of every citizen because, on the basis of this decision, they confiscated all the property of all citizens who were not in the territory in question. They confiscated both moveable and immovable property, and there were quite a few Serbs too who had left this territory because they did not agree with what was happening. However, it concerned everyone so the final fate, what finally happened, was that all property was confiscated, all the property of a person who had been amassing it throughout their life. In this way, such a person was prevented from returning to the territory, which was subjected to this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your experience, before this decision, had such a law existed, whereby property could be confiscated if a person didn't return?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, then, please, to the conclusion, set of conclusions numbered number 9, which in fact are dated the 13th of May? Item number 2, "Dr. Vukic is to submit his report on the work of the committee for standardising key staff at the Banja Luka clinical medical centre within three days." What in your experience did "standardising key staff" actually mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think he's shown that he has any experience in knowing what "standardising key staff" means. If there could be some foundation for that, that he has some special training that let's him know what those words mean, if they are words of legal art or something, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him tell us whether he knows what "standardising key staff" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I was asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure if he doesn't know what it means, he will obviously be referring to the corresponding words in his own language, as they appear in the government gazette, he's going to tell us, "I don't know." So if he knows, I think the question by Ms. Korner is very pertinent but obviously depends on whether the witness knows the answer to that question or not. So Mr. Dzonlic, obviously you have heard what Mr. Ackerman said. You have heard what I remarked afterwards. Ms. Korner for the Prosecution has asked you to comment on the words "standardising key staff," what they mean in particular. If you are in a position to tell us what they mean, if you have an idea at all of what was meant in that conclusion by "standardising key staff" as they appear in your own language in the B/C/S version of the government gazette, then tell us. If you're not in a position to answer the question, there is no problem, just tell us, "I'm not in a position to answer that question."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: See, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you -- Mr. Dzonlic, could you tell us, then, please, what was meant by that expression?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commission for the Standardisation of Staff, which was formed in all economic organisations, was formed with the objective, the main objective, of examining those who were employed within a certain period of time. We should return to my answer to the previous two questions perhaps. If a professional of non-Serbian nationality was given a wartime assignment or preserved his job according to a wartime assignment because there was no such person of Serbian nationality to occupy the post, then the Commission after a certain period of time had to examine whether he still met certain criteria that had been set by that Commission. They had to see whether there was a Serbian citizen who would be able to adequately replace a citizen of non-Serb nationality, and if this was determined by the Commission, then the citizen of non-Serbian nationality would be dismissed and would be replaced by a Serbian citizen. The Commission also had, as a task, had the task of monitoring the behaviour of such people, especially in hospitals, and as far as I can see, the person in question here is Dr. Vukic, who worked in the clinical centre, because wounded people would appear there, members of the Serbian army, Serbian citizens, Serbian nationals, and the Commission was very concerned about monitoring the work of all citizens who were of non-Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dzonlic, how did you find out about these committees?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which committees are you referring to? Do you mean commissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Commissions, I'm so sorry, commissions of standardisation of staff.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of doctors in Banja Luka who were Bosniaks, and they would speak about what was happening, especially in the clinical centre. My wife is also a doctor and I know this on that basis too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What actually happened to your wife? I'm sorry, I'll go back. Where was your wife working? At the clinical centre?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife wasn't working in the clinical medical centre. She worked in the health centre in Skender Vakuf. She was working in the emergency ward. And one day, her director - and this happened during this period - her director asked her to remain in the emergency service because she found it appropriate to work in shifts, one day from the morning until the evening, and the other day from the evening until the morning, and then she would be free for three days and would then go home. However, the director told her that the emergency service, that the ambulance service, had to be ethnically clean and that she could not remain there because of the people who were being brought in, because of the wounded soldiers, and for this reason, she left her job of her own free will and handed in her documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Can we move, staying with the same decision, number 9, to item number 4?" The security services in Banja Luka is to fully implement the decisions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on the disarming of illegal paramilitary units and individuals who are in possession of weapons and ammunition." Mr. Dzonlic, you've told us yesterday about the paramilitary groups you saw in Banja Luka. Were you aware of any attempt to disarm those units?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I spoke about paramilitary formations composed of citizens of Serbian nationality, because I considered them to be paramilitary formations as they weren't under the control of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as far as I can understand this decision, it does not refer to these formations but to -- it refers to all citizens, and to some other paramilitary formations of which I am not aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Then finally, on this one, this conclusion, item number 6, "The certificates issued by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina to individuals who are moving out of the territory of the autonomous region shall also be valued for their belongs, households items, furniture, clothes and motor vehicles." You gave a very lengthy description yesterday of the number of certificates that had to be issued. Are these the certificates that this decision refers to, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This does refer to those certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we could now move, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Yes, I got my pages out of order for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- to conclusion number 12? And look, please, at item number 9, which states, "Reciprocity" -- this is going to be a bit like mobilisation -- "should be applied in the resettlement of the population throughout the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, does reciprocity, does that have a specific legal meaning, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The word "reciprocity" has a very significant legal meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in this context, what do you understand this to mean?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this conclusion, for me, this means, in the first place, that the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Hercegovina, had already by then considered itself to be sovereign, a sovereign territory and an international legal entity. According to the knowledge I have, Reciprocity, the principle of reciprocity can be applicable on the basis of international law only between sovereign and internationally legally recognised entities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. De Roux? MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think now we are hearing an opinion, a legal opinion, not testimony here. And I think that what the witness thinks legally regarding the interpretation of the word "reciprocity" appears to me to be pure opinion and far from the testimony that we expect of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Ms. Korner, perhaps in a way, Mr. De Roux is right. You could perhaps rephrase the question, asking the witness what he understands by -- in this paragraph 9, "Reciprocity should be applied in the resettlement of the population," and we will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was going to come to that, Your Honour. May I point out that this gentleman is, in fact, a lawyer practising -- was a lawyer practising in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still is. And now he is legal adviser to the secretary of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just say that he was not represented by the Prosecution to be an expert witness. There is no written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. He's not being considered as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I would object to him being allowed to testify as an expert witness, because otherwise the Prosecution would have had to comply with the rules of this Tribunal regarding reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not giving evidence as an expert witness. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's not giving evidence as an expert witness. He's giving evidence as to the effect of these decisions and what his understanding is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, Mr. Dzonlic, in your -- was this decision -- what effect did that have?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us, this decision was absolutely unacceptable, and for us, it represented the engineering of ethnic cleansing within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, we never would have agreed to such a principle of resettlement and moving out of peoples, because it is impossible within an internationally recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And for us, it was absolutely null and void. But it was a form of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why do you say it was a form of ethnic cleansing? What was the practical effect?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say it would mean that within the territory of Republika Srpska, that territory would be absolutely Serb. If, shall we say, it had 1.000 Bosniaks, they would be resettled outside the territory of Republika Srpska, and a thousand Serbs would move into the territory of Republika Srpska. And that would be this process of complete ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then can we move, please, to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just checking on the statement, whether I need to look at the next --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Conclusion number 15, I'm sorry, dated the 22nd of May. Item number 2, "All flats that have been empty for over 15 days are to be taken over for housing the homeless." Before the Crisis Staff took over, was there any such provision in the law allowing flats that had been empty to be taken over?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of housing and housing rights was regulated by the law on -- I can't remember quite now, just now, the full name of the law, but I know that according to the law, the right to a dwelling may be withdrawn if the dwelling is not being used for longer than six months. If you're not living in your apartment without any justifiable cause for longer than six months, then the person who granted you housing rights could withdraw those rights, and not after 15 days, as it says in this conclusion. The name of the law was the Law on Housing Relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as a matter of practicalities again, what sort of housing did this law actually affect? In other words, to your knowledge, was housing taken over?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apartments were taken over en masse. All apartments which had been abandoned by the people who left Banja Luka, all those apartments were simultaneously taken over by Serbs, and very frequently even before the tenants had left Banja Luka, they were evicted from their homes, and only after that did they leave Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move, please, then, to number 17, item -- conclusion number 17, 26th of May? Item number 4 again deals with the standardisation of key staff, this time in the municipalities. And then item number 6, "An agency shall be established to work on the problem of population resettlement." Do you know whether such an agency was established?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the agency I referred to earlier on, known in town as Brdjanin's agency, and it was headed by Perka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Could you move to conclusion number 23, the 29th of May? Item number 1, "It has been decided that all Muslims and Croats who so wish should be able to move out of the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but on condition that Serbs living outside the Serbian autonomous districts and regions are allowed to move into the territories of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In this manner, an exchange of population or more precisely a resettlement of people from one part of the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to another would be carried out in an organised manner." And it goes on to talk about Muslims from Prijedor, Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi and Serbs in Central Bosnia who wanted to move but are not permitted by local authorities. And then it goes on to say, "The crisis staff has invited the SDA and the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina to become actively involved in facilitating a resettlement of the population." Now, the first question, Mr. Dzonlic, is this what you were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. referring to when we had the discussion about the conclusion that talked about reciprocity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says that the Crisis Staff had invited the SDA and the HDZ to become involved. Do you recall any such request being made to your party in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall. The Executive Board of the Banja Luka SDA discussed this request at a meeting it held, and we reached a resolute decision to oppose this method of resettlement and the engineering of ethnic cleansing of peoples. I do know that that was also the position of the official authorities, that is the HDZ party in Banja Luka, which also opposed this way of resettling the population. And we came to the conclusion that this should be published in the public media, to make it clear to the people that we were not in favour of ethnic cleansing and the organised resettlement of peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you able to publish this in the media?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was published, in the local newspapers. I think it was published. But I do know for certain that we decided that it should be published, and I think it was published in the local daily newspaper, Glas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, on this set of documents, could you go to conclusion number 26, Article 3. It's the 3rd of June meeting apparently. "Natural persons leaving the Autonomous Region of Krajina may take out a maximum of 300 Deutschmarks or corresponding amounts in other currencies which may not exceed this limit." You've told us yesterday, Mr. Dzonlic, about the limitations. How was this -- in your experience, how was the -- this particular decree or article enforced, namely that no one was allowed to take more than 300 Deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier on that Bosniaks of Banja Luka were economically independent and relatively well-off people. We knew of this limit of 300 Deutschmarks that could be taken out, but I also knew that people take -- took with them more than that, if they had it, and they hid the money in various ways. They concealed the funds they were taking with them. But there were quite a number of people who didn't have such means because they had been confiscated from them, either by force while they were still in Banja Luka, or they had spent it on all the certificates that I listed a moment ago in order to be given the document allowing their resettlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. That's all I have on that document. Can I ask that that be taken away from you and that you be given exhibit which has been numbered P258? It is in the binder volume 2 of the Banja Luka documents. And it had a disclosure number of 3.70. It's the second set of the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at number -- it's in slightly different format, this apparently, at number 32. Actually I'm sorry, could we just for a moment go to number 30? The first decision, 29, is signed by the president of the Crisis Staff, Radoslav Brdjanin. The next decision or article is signed by the president of the executive council, apparently, Nikola Erceg. You explained to us that the function of the executive council and that of the Crisis Staff yesterday. That decision apparently refers to an article in respect of sales tax and that like. What would be the reason, in your view, your knowledge, of Mr. Erceg as opposed to Mr. Brdjanin signing this decision?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the executive council was actually equal to the government, and that it takes technical and operational decisions, implementing the policies and conclusions adopted at the level of the Crisis Staff. The executive council enforces those decisions. And that is why this decision was signed by the president of the executive council and not the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. All right. Could we go on, then, please, to number 32? Which talks about a decision on the establishment of the Krajina Emigration Society and the next decision, number 33, also the 9th of June, saying that Zoran Malesevic was to be the Coordinator. Did you ever hear about something called the Krajina Emigration Society?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hear of it for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, then, please to number 35? Decision number 1? "Landlords who have rented or are renting out flats or parts of flats which are either the property of physical persons or are social property to tenants who are in the theatre of operations and under the command of the JNA, Yugoslav People's Republic and the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may not give the tenants and their families notice while they are still in the theatre of operations." First of all, can you just explain to us what is the difference between the property of physical persons or are social property?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A physical person may have had a privately owned house that he lived in and that was his house. He could also have bought an apartment in an apartment building and he could have been the owner of an apartment, as opposed to a socially owned apartment in which a physical person enjoys only the status of a tenant and he is not the owner of the apartment, but he may use it and dispose of it for the purpose of dwelling in it, and he may also subrent it. According to the law, he may rent only a part of the apartment, not the whole apartment. If he were to rent out the whole apartment, that would be a legal basis for his right to tenancy to be withdrawn from him. So he could have rented out a room with the right of the tenant to use the kitchen and the bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How much of property in Banja Luka, in June of 1992, was privately owned, roughly? I appreciate you can't give an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know it, tell us, if you don't just say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All houses were privately owned. As for flats or apartments, the majority were socially owned. Maybe only 10 per cent of the total housing was privately owned and 90 per cent was socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So if we understand this correctly, this decision was saying that people who were serving either under the command of the JNA or the army of the Serbian Republic, the VRS, could not be given notice at all?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of the JNA as opposed to the VRS, Bosnian Serb Army, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never absolutely certain about that, but I thought that there were members of the JNA present to distinguish them from members of the VRS because JNA members differed in terms of the uniforms they wore, and their uniform slightly differed from those of members of the Serbian army. So I assumed that they were members of the JNA, though I never knew that officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just very briefly perhaps before the break, what was the difference that you could see between the uniforms of the two?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was of better quality, shall I put it that way, the uniforms worn by JNA members, in terms of the material. It was more elegant, and they were always neat and properly clothed, like real soldiers. It was well ironed. And as I had served in the former JNA, I knew that the officers were always neat and orderly, like proper soldiers, as opposed to members of the Army of Republika Srpska, who were not so well dressed as these were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Your Honour, I only have one more item on this particular set of documents so whether Your Honour would wish me to deal with it now or after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mean, you're referring to the next document, P295?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, on this particular set of documents I'm just going to deal with one more conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, unless there is an objection from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we go ahead and then we break immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you go to item number 45 or conclusion number 45 in the same documents? A meeting on the 19th of June. Number 1, "The proper municipal organs of administration shall be informed of all abandoned property, which shall then be proclaimed property of the state and placed at the disposal of the municipal assemblies." In practical terms, Mr. Dzonlic, what effect did that decision have?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effects were similar as of the previous decision. The confiscation of all the property of citizens who were not within the territory of the region. So this decision also meant that all property which was privately owned should be proclaimed by decree state-owned property and placed at the disposal of the municipality, which meant a violation of a basic human right, the right to property, the right to personal, private property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before this, was there any provision in Bosnian law for such a -- let's see the word they used -- "removal" of property?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the existence of any such provisions, providing for this way of confiscating property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Your Honour, that's all I will ask on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. We will have a break until 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to apologise for the delay that I caused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem but I think once this matter has been brought up, let me make myself clear. The most part of these proceedings are public but there are moments when we go in closed session, and you will immediately understand the preoccupation of this Trial Chamber if at any moment while we are in closed session a -- there are mobile phones around in the courtroom. Please don't put me in a position, put us in a position, where we have to question or take steps or whatever. It's a gentlemen's and gentlelady's agreement that this certainly will not happen. I mean I know what use can be made of mobile phones and I hope we will not have to intervene. This is all I wanted to say. So it's -- I think -- I don't need to explain any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Its presence here was almost totally inadvertent. I almost always lock it in my locker. I just happened to forget this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I forgot several things this morning, Your Honour. The other thing I forgot this morning was my cross-examination notes which are still sitting in my printer at home, but that's okay. I can deal fine without them. I think for a while at least. The other thing that I need to report to you was that I think we have completed the work on the proposed calendar. I think all three parties have now agreed and that it is -- I think it's been provided to the Registry and it's now in your hands, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet, but almost. It's only about ten feet away. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I ought to admit that in Court in another jurisdiction my mobile phone actually went off in the middle of cross-examination. I think it's a problem common to everyone. Your Honour, may I just mention before Mr. Dzonlic comes back in that the -- I've been discussing with Mr. Ackerman the question of this newspaper article again because it's necessary for me to notify counsel instructed by the journalist, and can I digress for a moment? We had a call from what's called the Public Information Office here about this matter. It's perhaps my fault for mentioning the name of the journalist in court yesterday. I declined to give very much information because this matter is still pending but it might help if perhaps Your Honour were to say -- I don't know whether Your Honours have the power to do this -- but that until this matter is resolved, there should be no press publication at the moment. I'm not sure. In my jurisdiction the judges do have a power to prevent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is also usually a provision in the law providing for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which I don't think there is in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it may be that I can leave that for the moment. I was somewhat concerned because clearly at the moment this is still a matter that's under discussion in these proceedings, even though it's been done in open court. But there is a matter of law that Mr. Ackerman wishes to raise in respect of the admission, at all, of any of the articles. I wonder if it would be possible to do it, we remain in Your Honour's hands, either at the end of today, in other words disposing -- allowing Mr. Dzonlic to leave earlier, or first thing tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whatever you prefer. I think our first duty is to make sure that Mr. Dzonlic finishes his testimony as early as possible so that he may return to where he came from, and today is already Thursday so I don't know what to expect by way of cross-examination, but I don't anticipate from -- I'm not anticipating your cross-examination to finish, both of you, by the end of tomorrow's session, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm quite certain he'll be here on Monday just judging by the length of the direct and the amount of material that needs to be covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it more or less irrelevant whether we deal with this procedural, legal issue at the end of today's sitting or tomorrow morning, depending on whether the examination-in-chief finishes today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me suggest that we try to deal with it at 1.30. That would solve a couple of problems for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Provided Ms. Korner can terminate her examination-in-chief by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I anticipate finishing before the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that would be ideal then. Do you think we can deal with it in a quarter of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so. I think it's pretty straightforward and nothing very complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I just correct one thing that was brought to my attention in the break that I said this morning? Your Honour, the humanitarian organisation wishes to, before it grants its final permission, just to look at the terms of Your Honour's ruling and so I understand that this cannot be done because of the time gap until this afternoon so it will be tomorrow morning, that disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So I think we can bring in the witness. Yes, Ms. Korner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I'd like you now to be given, please, the next set of Official Gazettes, which are P295, disclosure number 3.71, the first document in volume 3 of the Banja Luka documents. And could you look, please, first at number 51, which is -- refers to a meeting of the executive council this time on the 30th of June, 1992? Conclusion number 1, "The government shall guarantee all the rights of individuals who have proved their patriotism in these difficult times regardless of their religion or nationality." Mr. Dzonlic, were in your experience, the rights of all individuals regardless of their religion or nationality guaranteed by the government?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the words "proved their patriotism"? How were nationalities, in your experience, to prove their patriotism?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People expressed their patriotism in specific cases by responding to the call-up to join the army of the -- Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and first of all to defend their state as they called it and secondly, by showing loyalty, by showing their patriotism by responding to the Serbian plebiscite, and to all the mobilisations that had been implemented. But the main thing was for someone to have responded, to have responded to the call-up to join the Army of Republika Srpska. In such cases they would consider such a person to be a patriot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of any so-called loyalty oath that had to be taken to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was required to take such a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that such an oath had to be taken by members of the police who worked in the state security service, the state security centre in Banja Luka. All those who were employed had to take an oath of loyalty, and those who didn't lost his right to work, and I know that there were several Bosniaks who took this oath of loyalty, who signed a pledge of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did that enable them to remain within the security services, the state security services?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a short period of time, they remained there, but in the end, they remained without work too, regardless of the fact that they had signed a pledge of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I now take you, please, to the decision number 62, please? It's not the content of the decision that's of any relevance but it's signed on this occasion. It's dated the 17th of July, 1992. It's signed by the president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Vojo Kupresanin. Now, you told us yesterday that you'd heard the name Kupresanin but you weren't sure of his position. Were you aware on the 17th of July that the assembly of the autonomous region had recommenced sitting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just digress for a moment and it's purely so Your Honour can see the connections? In one of the earlier decisions we looked at, there was -- which I didn't draw Your Honour's attention to, a passage that said the decisions of the Autonomous Region Crisis Staff must be submitted to the assembly for ratification. Your Honour there is a document which we haven't looked at yet and I'm not going to ask Your Honours to look it at the moment. It's disclosure number 2.275. It's actually in volume 2, dated the 17th of July. Your Honours have admitted it as P -- if I can find it -- P43. So I think it must have been one of the ones that Dr. Donia looked at - I see Ms. Gustin nodding - which shows the assembly reassembling and the ratification of the ARK Crisis Staff decisions -- I should say verification, is the way it's put.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to look finally on this document, please, at item number 66, or decision number 66, the 24th of July? Again this time it's the executive council and it's actually signed by somebody called the secretary of the Secretariat for Education, Science, Culture and Physical Culture, Zlatko Kolecevic, decision 1, "Full-time and part-time students who have not fully complied with the provisions of the law of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on total national defence may not enrol in two-year colleges and institutes of university education." What in practical terms, was the effect of that decision, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before answering this question, I would like to say that the person in question is Zlatko Kolecevic because I know this -- the person named. He worked as a professor in the secondary school in Banja Luka. In practical terms, this decision meant that most of the Bosniaks, the absolute majority of the Bosniaks and Croats weren't able to continue with their education because they did not respond to the mobilisation and in this manner, they were denied their right to education.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the law on total national defence referred to mobilisation? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to ask you about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document is not in the binders. It was referred to in his statement and we are going to hand out copies. Your Honours has been given them. They are disclosure -- they were attached to the witness statement and it's the Banja Luka -- the Official Gazette of the Banja Luka municipality, issue number 9. We understand we gave them to the Registry the other day.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What's the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does it have an exhibit number at this point, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I'm going to ask that it be made Exhibit P470.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonlic, you had a chance to look at this when you made your second statement. This is the Official Gazette of the municipality of Banja Luka. Can you explain the difference between this gazette and the ones we've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Official Gazette, as the title itself says, is the Official Gazette of the municipality of Banja Luka, of the organs of the Assembly, the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, the legal organs of power of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. This assembly is a legal organ of power. And this is the gazette of a legal organ of power which refers to the -- which concerns the territory of the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's the difference between the type of decisions taken by the ones we looked at earlier, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, either Crisis Staff or Regional Assembly, and these taken by the municipality assembly? In other words, what's the division between the levels of authority?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my opinion, the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff were binding for the legal organs of power too, and thus for the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. And in accordance with the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff, the municipal assembly had to adopt the decisions of the Crisis Staff and legally implement them in every day life. And for this reason, the municipal assembly adopted such decisions, decisions such as the ones that are published in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your view -- having been there -- and having looked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Maitre de Roux, yes, please. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to raise the same objection as I made earlier on. In this case again, we are dealing with opinions that we are asking of the witness with regard to the way that he interprets the text. This witness is not an expert witness. He has to give testimony with regard to facts. And we are asking him for legal opinions, and for this reason, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not asking him for a legal opinion. I'm asking him from his own practical experience, living in the municipality, as a lawyer, what the difference was between the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff of the region and the municipality Crisis Staff or assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think Maitre de Roux, I think I have to allow him to answer that question, because he is not being asked the question as an expert witness. Please do remember that he was at the time already a lawyer, he was also a functionary, a higher officer, official of the SDA, and therefore this type of question being directed to him is perfectly legitimate and if he is in a position to answer it, he can answer it. It may well end up being his own personal interpretation of the significance of whatever is being asked from him, but it is certainly not being asked and forthcoming as or by way of an expert witness. I mean, he's just another witness who happens to be a lawyer, and he is not being -- in other words, the Trial Chamber is not taking his evidence as expert witness. It's just his personal, legal interpretation of the circumstances or, in this particular case, the -- he is explaining what he understood to be the difference between the municipality of Banja Luka decision-making process and the -- in the application or executing of the decisions of the ARK crisis. So I think I can, without any difficulty, allow it. Thank you. You may proceed. MR. DE ROUX: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I want to make this absolutely clear. From your experience as a citizen of Banja Luka, and having looked at the various documents, including the two gazettes, what decisions had more effect on the daily life in Banja Luka, those taken by the municipality, Predrag Radic, or those taken by the Crisis Staff or the assembly headed by Mr. Brdjanin or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions taken by the Crisis Staff had a greater impact because they were in the form of orders, as compared to those taken by the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. That assembly necessarily had to make certain decisions such as this one in the Official Gazette because once the Crisis Staff established a certain strategy, then it would make the decision that the legal authorities should implement those decisions, because, according to the laws, the positive regulations in force at the time, the municipal assembly had a great deal of authority regarding decision-making so that the Crisis Staff made it binding upon the municipal assembly to implement the decisions and thereby achieve the goals of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've looked at and you've explained a number of effects of the decisions taken by the Crisis Staff. We haven't gone through everything but from what you saw in your examination of the papers, were those decisions practically put into effect in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have seen that most of those decisions were put into effect. We've covered quite a number of decisions of the Crisis Staff now which affected life in Banja Luka and all of this was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to look at one or two matters that were dealt with by the municipality of Banja Luka. Could we look, please, at decision number 213? This is a decision, Article 1, relates to new names. It's dated the 16th of July and it's signed at the end by Predrag Radic, leader of the municipal council. New names, it says, have been determined for the following streets, and it gives a list. What was happening here, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there was a campaign on that Serbs believed, and I said that at the beginning, they would even say that we were breathing Serbian air, that even the air was Serbian. The Serbs took the decision to change the names of all streets, not just streets but also of schools and all other institutions, which historically speaking were not in line with their current policies. So that in article one of decision 213, they changed the name of the main street, Marsal Tito Street and Marsal Tito was a positive figure in the former Yugoslavia, they changed it to King Peter Karadjordjevic 1st Street, Kralj Petar Karadjordjevic. And this happened to all street names. The aim being, Serbifying all of them and eliminating all traces of positive history in the territory of the former Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next can we look at, please, decision number 216? Which was dated 7th of July? No, I'm sorry. It was a date -- yes. We -- if we read that, "In accordance with Article 240 of the statute of the municipality of Banja Luka Official Gazette, and Article 6 of the decision on the organisation and operation of the municipal council and its offices, and other offices of local government in the circumstances of war or imminent threat of war," and can we just pause there for a moment? You told us yesterday, I believe, or maybe the day before, that a Crisis Staff came or War Staff came into existence prior to this period, 1992, in an emergency situation. Had you heard the expression in circumstances of war or imminent threat of war before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only in emergency situations, but not the threat of war. In emergencies, and those emergencies were in fact listed, natural disasters, fires, floods, earthquakes, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this is a decision on restrictions of playing of music in outdoor places and bars and so on and so forth. On the face of it, it looks like a noise restriction decision. In practical terms, what was the effect of this, Mr. Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this way, human rights were being violated on the one hand, and on the other, there was a great deal of fear among people who had their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. own businesses, because, as a result of this decision, the police would enter those businesses on the grounds of this decision, and they would mistreat people simply because, allegedly, music was being played. On the other hand, in this way, they wanted to raise the morale among the people, to give the impression that there was no loud music and that there was law and order in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.
