If we can move, now, to decision number 217, which refers to a decision that Article 1, taxation, "Persons working abroad shall pay 100 Deutschmarks or the same amount in dinars towards their taxes and the money raised through this tax is intended for the Defence of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." When you looked at this, could you see any connection with any of the decisions taken by the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid I'm going to ask you to have back the first set of Official Gazettes. I've forgotten the exhibit number again. 227.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if one goes to conclusion number 14, item number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, I'm sorry, I interrupted you to address Their Honours. Were you able to see the connection there between a decision of the Crisis Staff and this decision?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to remember just now, there is a decision of the Crisis Staff on taxation and method of payment of taxation, and that the municipalities were charged to implement that decision. And the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka passed such a decision in accordance with the previously issued decision of the Crisis Staff on the method of payment of taxation. And that is how I see the link between the Crisis Staff and the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask about that document, and then finally, I would like Mr. Dzonlic to look at one last document. Your Honours, again this was attached to his statement. It's attachment number 13. I think Your Honours were given -- should have been given -- it's marked P471.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonlic, this is an announcement to the media from the Serbian Democratic Party, the Banja Luka Municipal Board and it's signed as we can see, by the president, Dr. Vukic, dated the 23rd of October, 1991, and it talks about the postponement of a rally to the 26th of October, 1991. Do you remember that rally?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not attend the meeting -- rally, but it was covered by the media quiet extensively and we were able to follow on the radio and on our TV screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What do you remember about that particular rally?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was attended by a large number of people. It is a large square in front of the department store, called Boska, in Banja Luka. I remember that there were quite a number of Serbian flags. I remember that some people climbed on to the nearby Palace Hotel, a part of which was still under construction so people climbed up and waved Serbian flags from the building. I remember that there were cries that this was Serbia, there were speeches held by individuals like Predrag Radic. I remember him speaking. And I assume that these others also spoke. And they said that this was part of Serbia and part of Yugoslavia, and that it will -- it would always remain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What effect did that have on you watching this rally?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that things could not be the way they put it, because already then the former SFRY no longer existed. Slovenia and Croatia had become independent states. And I know that a referendum was being prepared on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and according to my estimate, I knew that the majority of the people would opt for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I assumed that a war could break out. Of course, I never imagined that it would take the course that it did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Dzonlic, that's all I want to ask you about the documents. And I just have a couple of other topics to deal with. You told us that you left Banja Luka in February of 1993. Before you left in February, 1993, did you ever receive any form of ill treatment or harassment personally from the authorities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what form, first of all, ill-treatment, what form did that take?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time this was, I think, between -- between five and seven soldiers entered the apartment of my father in Djure Djakovica Street in Banja Luka where I was living. They forced their way in. My father was inside, my mother, my wife, and myself. They separated us into the different rooms. My father in the living-room. My mother to one room. Me in a second room. And my wife in the dining-room. And they cross-examined us and searched the apartment and they asked for my brother. At the time, my brother was at the Manjaca camp. They turned everything upside down in the apartment. On the balcony we had a sack of flour which they emptied out thinking that perhaps we were hiding something inside. They behaved rudely. They didn't beat us but they were very rude. And that was the first time. And it is difficult for me to say exactly when it happened, but I know that it was sometime between the 6th and 9th month of 1992. The next time, the civilian police came to the apartment. Inside, my wife and I were inside. And they said that I had to go with them. I did so. I started getting dressed. And just then my mother and father were at our neighbour's and by the time we got ready, when my mother and father came back, they found us preparing to leave. I asked that my father go with us. They agreed to that and said that they were taking me to the Military Secretariat. We got into a police car. I was immediately suspicious, seeing the civilian police car taking me to the Military Secretariat, so I thought this strange. My father and I got in at the -- on the back seat and they didn't drive us towards the military secretariat but in the direction of the Laos district which is in the opposite direction. So at the time I thought that they were going to kill us because they were driving in the opposite direction. However, they told us that they had to go in that direction because of an incident that had occurred, and indeed an incident had occurred. A man was beating a woman and when they had dealt with it, they drove us back to the Secretariat. There, I was interrogated. They told me that they had called me in allegedly because of a military uniform that I had been issued as a former member, as actually somebody who had served in the army of the former SFRY, and upon completing military service I was issued a uniform. But as I have already said, I had returned that uniform through my father. And then they let me go a couple of hours later. Then it happened once more. I don't know whether it was two or three of them that came to the apartment. And they took that certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wonder if that could be put in a time frame because we need to know whether we are in the confines of the indictment or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. At the first instance he said sixth to ninth month of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other one we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Dzonlic, pinpoint more or less the second incident when you were taken to the military station, when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This second incident may have occurred in the month of October, 1992, the tenth month, October or November. I really cannot state explicitly whether it was, but as far as I can remember, it was October or November. And the last time they came to the apartment, whether it was two or three policemen, I'm not sure, they were -- they treated us roughly. One of them even kicked me. And then they took from me this certificate, this permission to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... time was this that this happened and he's telling us what happened on that incident rather than when it happened. I think we need to know when it happened before he goes forward with what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has heard you already state the reasons why you are asking for a reference to the time span or the date, if it is at all possibility to pinpoint that, the reason being we have to know whether it falls within the time span of the indictment. But I see no difficulty at all in letting him finish the answer first and he will tell us the date afterwards. As soon as he finishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, can you just tell us when the last visit was, before Mr. Ackerman objects again?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This third time that they came, I think happened at the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993. It may have been in January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You left Banja Luka on the 26th of February, 1993. Can you remember roughly how long before your leaving this third visit by the police was?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a month prior to that, maybe -- maybe a month before, this third incident therefore was in January. So maybe a month prior to my leaving. Maybe around the 20th of January, as I left on the 26th, then it could have been the 25th of January, but I can't remember the exact date. I think it was sometime within that period. At the end of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In any event, Mr. Dzonlic, I was about to stop you. You had these three visits by the police. At any stage during those visits, were you ever -- you've mentioned being kicked, but ever really physically beaten up by the police officers, whether military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't beat me. They didn't beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've spoken about all the restrictions that took place in Banja Luka and the dismissals and the like. You've told us also that you heard about what happened in Prijedor and other places. In your experience, living in Banja Luka during this period of 1992 until you left in February, 1993, can you see an explanation for why what happened in other municipalities did not happen in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some explanation, some experience, that might explain why the same thing didn't happen in Banja Luka, the same thing as what happened in the immediate vicinity of Banja Luka did not happen in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Banja Luka is a fairly large town. It's the headquarters of the whole area. There were representatives in Banja Luka and there were headquarters there, the headquarters of the International Red Cross, and the UNHCR had its headquarters there, as well as the monitors of the European Union. And as a result, the Serbs were not able to do what they did in certain other towns. Secondly, in my opinion, this organised and developed plan of ethnic cleansing was made, having taken Banja Luka as an example. The Serbs did not need to commit terrible crimes and killings in Banja Luka because they organised on a weekly basis, every week, the deportation, the expulsion, of the non-Serbian population from Banja Luka. And in this manner, they gradually and quietly cleansed the city, and as a result, they did not need to do what they did in Prijedor and Kozarac and in other places. Similarly, I think that the Serbs felt that they were far more powerful, especially in Banja Luka, because Banja Luka is or Banja Luka was the logistics base of the former JNA and of the Serbs in Banja Luka, because, as far as I know, there were about ten large military barracks there. And another reason, Banja Luka is a very particular city because the non-Serbian population, at least as far as the Bosniaks are concerned, they all lived in the city. All the surrounding villages were Serbian villages. So that in that respect, they were quite sure that the Bosniaks in Banja Luka would not be able to put up any kind of resistance in the event of conflict. And I think that in this way they wanted to show the international community and the world that what was said was being done was not correct and they wanted to provide Banja Luka as an example. They wanted to provide Banja Luka as an example of the possibility of peaceful co-existence. And I think that this is the reason for which they didn't do the same things that they did in other cities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzonlic. Finally, you left on the 26th of February, 1993. Were you able to leave openly?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to leave openly. After people -- other people, after the procedure, were able to leave with a permit, but as I said earlier on, this permit was taken from me, and I was not able to leave in this way. I was not able to leave Banja Luka in this way. And I think it is important to mention this too. When my permit to leave was taken away, my wife and I went to the Secretariat for National Defence in the municipality of Banja Luka. We went to see the secretary, whose name was Denic. We said we would be coming and we asked to be received by him. We waited for quite a long time before he saw us. My wife asked Mr. Denic why my permit to leave Banja Luka had been taken away. He said, "Madam, it's a war. You should be happy that you are alive. I have been ordered -- I have been given orders not to let him leave Banja Luka." When I heard this, I said, "Thank you." And I told my wife that we should leave. And we left. So I was not able to, in inverted commas, leave legally, but I managed to leave in a very strange way. I managed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think you did tell us earlier, although I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, when was your -- the permit you'd obtained to leave removed from you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took my permit from me, I'm not sure whether it was in January or towards the end of 1992. I can't be precise about this, about when the police came, police in civilian clothing, they came into my house. They took that permit from me and they said that I had to give Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them this permit for departure. I'm not sure whether it was at the end of 1992 or at the beginning of 1993, but I think it was during this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, very shortly, Mr. Dzonlic, how did you actually leave Banja Luka? You can tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they took my permit, I became aware of the fact that after what Mr. Denic had told me, that I was forbidden to leave and I became worried. I then decided to report to the municipal Red Cross in the municipality of Banja Luka, and to go there with an application to go towards Novski and Okucani in the direction of Zagreb. I officially reported there but a colleague of my wife, who was related, she was a cousin of Perka who ran that agency, my wife asked that colleague of hers to organise departure through Perka and to enable us to get to Travnik, but the condition was not to be put on the official record because they would forward this record to the state security service. And my mother and wife went to Perka. My mother gave Perka 500 German marks so that she wouldn't put us on the list. This is how I entered the convoy but I was officially on the list for Novska but I went in a completely different direction and I managed to enter other territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dzonlic, I barely need to explain this to you because you are a lawyer, and an experienced and very capable lawyer from what I have seen, it's now the turn of the Defence teams to start their cross-examination. First cross-examination is forthcoming from the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin. And the attorney is Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dzonlic, how are you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This -- I'm going to talk to you first about what you talked about just a moment ago. You went through a very long explanation of why conditions in Banja Luka were so much different from other towns and villages in the area. And one of the things you talked about was that there was such an international presence there that it was important to create a situation in Banja Luka to make it appear that bad things were not happening, correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wasn't it obvious to these international people that there were bad things happening with all of the people that were living on the street who had been thrown out of their apartments?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't notice these people in the streets. People weren't sleeping in the streets. If someone had been expelled from his flat, he would have a cousin and he would go and stay with this cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So people weren't made homeless, in other words?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were made homeless but our people, Bosniaks, are charitable, the people are humane and they want to help each other and very glad to receive friends, acquaintances. And all these people who were expelled were made homeless because when I am living with someone else, that's not my house. I'm just there temporarily. All those who were forced out were made homeless, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did all of the Serb refugees coming into Banja Luka who had been forced out of Croatia and various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where were they living? Were they on the streets or in homes or what?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you know there were thousands and thousands of Serb refugees coming into Banja Luka, don't you, who were being thrown out of Croatia and other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. In 1992, there weren't any Serbs coming, and they weren't forced out from Banja Luka, forced to -- forced out to Croatia to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would you take the position that Serbs weren't forced out of Muslim municipalities like the Konjic municipality in 1992, early 1992, April, May?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Serbs were forced out of the municipality of Konjic. I'm not aware of this fact. But I have my personal position with regard to this. I don't think they were forced out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you concede that Muslim -- that Serbs were forced out of any Muslim municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know nothing, I take it, about, for instance, the liberation of a village called Bradina, in the Konjic municipality, by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided again with Exhibit P470, which is the Official Gazette, Banja Luka municipality, for 20 July?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- if I have it, could I formally ask that those two exhibits, P470 and P471 be admitted? I think I said it as we were going through, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did already. Yes, they are being admitted as exhibits, P470 and the other one was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P471. And I'm reminded that we put in the video of religious destruction. Could that be P472? And there is -- yet another version of that Banja Luka map, it will have to have a separate exhibit number, Your Honour, so that will be P2.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, you should now have before you the Official Gazette of the municipality of Banja Luka of 20 July, 1992. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when Ms. Korner began to ask you about that document, she was asking you about the relative positions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region and the municipality of Banja Luka, and you indicated that the municipality of Banja Luka would have been required to implement the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff. I believe that was kind of the preamble to your testimony regarding this document, this gazette from the municipality of Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's just look at these decisions. Let's start on page 1 with number 199. The first thing I would like to draw your attention to is the first paragraph there. The first paragraph sets out the basis for the decision that's being made, does it not, in accordance with what act, things of that nature? So, for instance, with 199, it's in accordance with Article 114 of the urban development act of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Article 240 of the statute of the municipality of Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No where in that paragraph does it say, "And pursuant to a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina," does it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please look at number 200 on the next page. No reference to the Crisis Staff in that first paragraph, is there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a reference to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 202 on the next page, no reference to the Crisis Staff, is there, the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Decision 204, what happened to 203? In any event, decision 204, no mention of the ARK Crisis Staff, is there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 205, any mention of the ARK Crisis Staff as a basis for the decision?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 206, same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, may I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you simply ask the witness to go through the document one decision after the other himself without the need of putting question repeatedly one time after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will tell us at the end whether he, in this document, he notices that a decision is being taken by way of implementation of a previous decision of the ARK crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing for him to do that, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of the day it still doesn't mean that any decision is not by way of implementation because you don't need to state each time that you are implementing the decision of someone else. That could be implied from the kind, the nature, the quality of the decision taken as was the case with one of the decisions that Ms. Korner questioned the witness about, namely, the taxation, the 300 Deutschmarks or 100 Deutschmark taxation for those living, for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We will be coming to that, Your Honour, definitely be coming to that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can look at these decisions very quickly and see from the introductory part, whether in any of these decisions, there is a preliminary statement saying that it is by way of implementation or execution of the decision of the ARK crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he's now done that and can probably answer you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just simply this, Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman having said what happened to 201, there is a 201 in the original, and I'm sorry, I mean, we are in the same position, we can't physically check every translation, but if anybody wants -

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 203 is the one I was trying to find.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a 203 as well in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not in the translation either, nor is -- Your Honour, if anybody thinks it's worth it, then we will have to send it back for translation. I mean, I'm reluctant to but there has been a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is one of the final translations. This is not a draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were better off when we had a draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the drafts are better, Your Honour, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, point taken, Ms. Korner, if we need to have those two documents translated, we will have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if either of the numbers that has not been translated refers to a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, then I think it probably should be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't tell you that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I can't read --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will have it read through in the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, have you looked through all of these decisions as the Judge has suggested?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read through all of them but I have read through the majority of them and I can see that in the preamble of the decision, no reference is made to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And under the law regarding the making and writing of decisions, it is required that one state in the preamble the basis upon which the decision is being made, isn't it? Isn't that legally required?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let's go to number 213, that Ms. Korner referred you to. Have you found that one?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is the one that you referred to as the Serbs changing the names of streets to Serb names, and basically stamping their territory as Serbian territory. That was basically your testimony, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who Kralj Petar Karadjordjevic is?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's King Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the change there is from the Marsal Tito Street, which is -- everybody knows who he was, to the King Petar Street then; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at the second one. Who is Mose Pijade; do you know?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who is Mose Pijade

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mose Pijade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mose Pijade was a former partisan in the Second World War. He was part of the resistance, the resistance against the fascist aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was he a Serb or Croat or a Muslim or what?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a Jew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the street was changed to Jewish Street, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not a Serbian street name, then, is it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a name at all. It designates a membership of people. It's not a person's name, because Jewish is not the name of a person. It just designates a membership of a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was not changed to a Serbian street name, was it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, it's not a Serbian name of a particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me to save sometime, let me have you look at the rest of them, three through nine. Are those all situations where streets that had non-Serbian names were changed to Serbian names? Do you want to say that that's the case with every one of those?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 8, the name it gives is Skender Kulenovic [phoen]. His nationality is Bosniak and his name is there. That is not a Serbian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they changed a street to a Bosniak name; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could we go now to decision 216, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. We will break right now, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 to 1.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, we were looking at decision 216, and you have that in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this is the decision you said was oppressive against non-Serbs because it allowed the police to go inside businesses and harass people for playing music. That's basically your testimony, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they had a negative attitude toward the Serbs. I said that it had a negative impact on the owners of catering establishments and Bosniaks and Croats owned quite a number of such private establishments. And I said that it enabled the Serb police on these grounds to enter those private businesses and to disturb them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's look first at the first paragraph under Article 1. That paragraph bans the playing of music outdoors, outside of bars, in the streets and squares, and pedestrian areas. That's what it bans, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second one deals only with bars, "Playing music inside bars, is allowed at a reasonable volume so that it does not disturb passersby and tenants"; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess you would agree that you would -- you might find that kind of a law, that kind of a statute, in almost any city in the world that has noise ordinances, noise restriction laws, probably you have it here in The Hague, don't you guess?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at 217, the next decision. Now, I take it, Mr. Dzonlic, that you were handed this Official Gazette of the municipality of Banja Luka of July 20, 1992, and as -- and asked to look through this and see if you could find any indication that the Banja Luka municipality had followed any decisions or conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff. I assume you were asked to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you found was the decision at 217, which says "Persons working abroad shall pay 100 Deutschmarks or the same amount in dinars toward their taxes"; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the decision -- actually it's not a decision. Let me find it. There is a conclusion of the ARK Crisis Staff which is contained in issue number 2 of the ARK gazette, as that which is Prosecution Exhibit what? I've forgotten. I should have written it on here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's 227, P227. I think. I did have a list myself. I've thrown mine away, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We think it's 227, but in any event --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 255, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you need to look at 255 or can you recall that decision -- conclusion, actually, where the Crisis Staff decided to introduce a tax for workers abroad in the amount of 100 Deutschmarks or the equivalent amount in dinars? Do you recall that that's the case in the Crisis Staff conclusion, do you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the conclusion of the Crisis Staff on taxation but that conclusion did not specify the amount of the tax. The municipality did that. It specified the amount of the tax and established that it should be 100 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Provide the witness, please, with Prosecution Exhibit 255. Everybody is shaking their heads as if there is no such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. It was the first document that was exhibited when Mr. Dzonlic -- this was initially it was described to us or indicated to us as going to be document P339. That was the disclosure number. In reality, then, it came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's P255. This is the decision of the Crisis Staff of the 22nd June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm so sorry, it's my error. I think we will find it's 227. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P227, disclosure number 3.69.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's actually my fault, Your Honour, not Ms. Korner's because I should keep better track of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As long as we've sorted it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll direct you in that document to conclusion number 14. Did you find it? Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it says, "The Crisis Staff has decided to introduce a tax for workers abroad in the amount of 100 Deutschmarks or the equivalent amount in dinars"; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that tax would have been payable to whom? To what government was that tax payable?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this conclusion of the Crisis Staff, it is not indicated to whom it should be payable to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, since the Crisis Staff was taking the place of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the only organ that they could order a tax paid to would be the Autonomous Region of Krajina; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all payments went to the Defence Ministry, even we, as I said before, were obliged to make a payment of 350 Deutschmarks addressed to the Defence Ministry when leaving Banja Luka, and all taxes were channelled into the financing of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know exactly to which account this was to be payable, but I think that it went to the account of the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you're correct, if all taxes went to the Defence Ministry, then the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina had no money with which to function. Couldn't pay staff, couldn't do anything; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not find, do you, anywhere in this conclusion, that that 100 Deutschmarks is to be paid to the Defence Ministry?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in the conclusion of the Crisis Staff, dated the 21st of May, 1992, I cannot see to whom these funds are payable. I just see that the obligation is established for the payment of that sum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And I want to ask you the question that you didn't answer a moment ago. That's this: The Crisis Staff, as you have told us, was a substitution for the ARK assembly, and as such, the Crisis Staff could not order a tax to be paid to anybody but the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That would have been their only competence. They couldn't have ordered a tax paid to the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. They couldn't make a tax being paid to the Netherlands. I think they couldn't even order this decision to be obliged -- to oblige all citizens in other states, that is, that the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if they are working in the Netherlands, they should pay tax to the Netherlands and not to a third country, especially not the Bosnian Krajina or Bosnia-Herzegovina. A tax is paid where an income is obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this tax, at least, could not have gone beyond the confines of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, could it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been paid through commercial banks anywhere in the world, but it was intended for the needs of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. If it was paid and it could have been -- the payment could have been made through commercial banks anywhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This conclusion is dated 21 May, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was located in Banja Luka, was it not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look now at the other document, P470, the Official Gazette of the municipality of Banja Luka, at decision 217, the first thing I will draw your attention to is the date of that decision, 16 July, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, you said decision 216?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the one that talks about persons working abroad shall pay 100 Deutschmarks or the same amount in dinars. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I just don't see the date of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just look up above the word "decision". It says it was passed at its meeting on 16 July, 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that's almost two months after the Crisis Staff conclusion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you still want to take the position that the decision of the municipal assembly on 16 July is in response to a May decision of the -- conclusion of the ARK Crisis Staff? Do you still want to take that position? That it took them two months to get around to this?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I still believe that. The decision was probably passed earlier but it was published on the 16th, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says -- it says --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what it says; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Meeting on the 16th of July, passed a decision. Not earlier than that, right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I still stand by what I said, and I do link it to the decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in this entire edition of the Official Gazette of 20th of July, 1992, you find no other decision of the Banja Luka municipality that you can link to any conclusions of the Crisis Staff, do you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner was asking you about the difference between conclusions of the Crisis Staff and decisions of the Banja Luka municipality. And, Ms. Korner, for your purposes, I'm reading from an answer that's at LiveNote 43, line 1, at 11.34.52 this morning. Your answer, Mr. Dzonlic, to her question was: "The decisions taken by the crisis staff had a greater impact because they were in the form of orders." Now, the first thing I want to you do is go back now to that document that you were looking at earlier, which I think we've decided was 227. It's the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina of 5 June, 1992. I'd like you to just, on your own, look through that and tell me if you see any document in there that is called an order, or if it isn't simply a few decisions and a lot of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and all the decisions it contains? The first decision, a general public mobilisation is ordered throughout the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that is signed by Lieutenant Colonel Sajic; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second one that's called a decision is signed by Nikola Erceg; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you come to documents that are called conclusions. There are one -- two of those; right?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to go through all of these. I want to go on with your answer now after the word "orders." "The decisions taken by the Crisis Staff had a greater impact because they were in the form of orders as compared to those taken by the municipal assembly of Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at those of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, which is P470, that's the 20 July, 1992, edition of the Official Gazette, and you have that there in front of you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Starts with --

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Starts with 199 and through 243. If you look at the very back, there is an index which will help you.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Every one of those documents with maybe one exception is a decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You go on with your answer, "That assembly," referring to the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly, "Necessarily had to make certain decisions such as this one in the Official Gazette because once the Crisis Staff established a certain strategy, then it would make the decision that the legal authorities should implement those decisions because, according to the laws, the positive regulations in force at the time." What were the laws and positive regulations in force at the time, July 20th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the positive regulations that existed. We see in the decisions, in the Official Gazette of Banja Luka municipality, specifically the law on urban development, for instance. That is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. frequently referred to because according to that law, it was only the municipal assembly that could implement decisions linked to urban development and not the Crisis Staff, and that is why reference here is to the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. They couldn't change the law on urban development so that this should be done instead of by the municipal assembly by the Crisis Staff. So then there is frequent mention of this act, Urban Development Act. Now, let's look further. The law on expropriation, on construction land, et cetera. These are the positive regulations that were in force then and are in force even today, and they were taken over from the former SFRY and accepted as generally applicable, many of which are still valid to this day, some with minor changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your statement that the municipality of Banja Luka needed to comply with the laws and positive regulations in force at the time referred to basically what we see in these preambles and just, for instance, in the first one, 199, the Urban Development Act, which you talked about, is an act of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it appears in the Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said it has to conform with the law. According to those laws, it was competent for such acts, regulatory provisions regarding land development. And it was the municipal assembly that is competent for the implementation of decisions on land development and that is why it took such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but what I'm really trying to refer you to is decision 199. They say the decision is being made in accordance with Article 114 of the Urban Development Act, which is apparently an act of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, the assembly of SRBiH, I would assume; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm not going to go through each one of these but many of these decisions refer to that Urban Development Act, don't they, of the SRBiH?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In your testimony on your first day here, you were talking with Ms. Korner about the issue of mobilisation, and people who failed to respond to mobilisation and what would happen to those who failed to respond, and at page 2310 of the transcript, you were asked this question: "What about those of Serb ethnicity who did not respond?" Your answer was: "As far as I know not a single Serbian citizen was subjected to proceedings of any kind." Do you recall that answer?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, up to a point. I remember saying something like that. I don't know that any citizen of Serb ethnicity was exposed to any kind of torture or suffered any consequences because of failure to respond to the mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your answer was proceedings of any kind, and then you proceeded to talk about charges brought against people who you represented and that some of them were charged in military courts where the sentences were severe, and some in misdemeanour courts where the sentences were fines. You recall that whole bit of conversation, do you not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to be shown DB -- Exhibits DB50A, 51A and 52A, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While he is waiting to be shown these documents, Mr. Ackerman, may I remind you of the arrangement we have to dedicate the last quarter of an hour to discuss the issue, the legal issue, that you wanted to raise? So I leave it to you to decide or show me a preference, whether you would like to stop now and raise the matter or continue with your cross-examination now that you have sort of opened a new parenthesis and have your submissions on the legal matter tomorrow morning? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that this can be done, what I'm doing right now, can be done in about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to try to do it in about two minutes, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dzonlic, what you're being shown are three documents, and I'll simply ask you aren't these criminal charges brought against Serbs for failing to respond to the mobilisation in the military court? I think you can answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are criminal charges. This is a report which wants to institute proceedings, but whether or not proceedings were instituted, I do not know. This is just a criminal report, perhaps from the Secretariat of Defence. I don't know who was the originator. But I don't think criminal proceedings were instituted, if I have understood you well. This is just a criminal report for not responding to mobilisation, and it is against the persons who have been named in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say criminal report. It says "criminal charges," does it not? "Krivicnu prijavu" is criminal charges, correct? Not "criminal report"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR DZONLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think this is a good time to stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Dzonlic, once more, the Trial Chamber thanks you for your patience and your cooperation throughout the whole of this morning, as it was the case yesterday and the day before. I'm afraid your task is not over as yet. Your presence is needed again tomorrow. And I take it that probably, in all probability, we will not even finish tomorrow with you. So be prepared that you may have to stay -- to come back on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you once more. And you may now leave the courtroom. You will be escorted of course. Thank you. In the meantime, please, the same advice or warning that I gave you yesterday and the day before, that you are not to communicate with anyone regarding the -- and we will see you tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Ackerman, do you want to wait until the witness is out or can we start straight away?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, these documents were handed to us one minute before Your Honours sat. Understand from Mr. Ackerman that these are the documents he referred to the other day, which he had just been sent from Banja Luka. The explanation is, as I understand it, without a translation, he can't judge whether or not they are going to be relevant. Your Honour, I do not accept that. I do not accept that, as I have already pointed out once in Court and certainly to Mr. Ackerman, he has on his team no less than two people who both read and understand and write the language. It must be clear whether or not there is an official translation, that these documents are going to be used. Your Honour, rightly, Mr. Ackerman and Defence team for Mr. Talic have objected if we didn't give lists of documents. The same must apply. In addition, in relation to these particular documents, having heard the witness's answer, before I agree that that they should be admitted and seek to argue them. I want to know exactly what these documents are, where they come from, and obviously whether it is the results of any Prosecution, if there were a Prosecution, because the witness's answer is that these are not anything further than a report with a view to proceedings, what the up shot was. Now, clearly, my learned friends have access to documents or information, but at the moment, I object to these documents being admitted if they are being put forward as proof that Serbs were actually prosecuted. And I certainly would like, in future, please, to receive -- I've already indicated, we are happy to receive the documents untranslated, if it is known that they are going to be used and that, at the time when they will be used they will be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, these witnesses frequently don't have in their statements the things that require investigation, and this witness said for the first time on 26 February that not a single Serbian citizen was subjected to proceedings of any kind. It's only at that point that I can say to an investigator, "Check this out and tell me whether there is any information of that nature." Fortunately it was able to be checked out rather quickly and I stood up when those documents arrived and told you that I had them and told you that I couldn't use them with the witness because they hadn't been translated and there was no opportunity with the witness that was here before to get them translated in time and that I would have it done as quickly as I could and furnish them to the Prosecutor and they were brought to me by the translator at the last break. I didn't expect them to be here even today. I thought that I'd probably have to use them when we got to the Defence case because of the lack of speed in the translation business. I can't do any better than conduct investigations when I hear the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Ackerman, your explanation in so far as it tries to impression the Trial Chamber that the need to instruct an investigator to make queries, find out whether the witness's statement was correct or not only arose two days ago. That I can understand. I also understand that in a way, you were fortunate that, or rather we were fortunate, that these three documents were dug up, found, almost immediately. Where I disagree with you, and I have to concede the point to Ms. Korner is that even on the face of these three documents, you had two words which you faced the witness with, namely "kivicnu prijavu," which to you means "criminal charges." You also had names which your two colleagues could easily identify as being of Serbian or not of Serbian origin, and at that point in time, regardless of the translation issue or problem, you, perhaps for the future, you could have shown towards each other more flexibility and said, "These three documents, on the face of them, seem to be relevant. I intend to use them pending furnishing you with a translation and photocopying the original as received in B/C/S language." In the meantime the Prosecution will be prepared in anticipation of the translation that you will be furnishing. Because I suppose that inside the remaining part of this Tribunal, they also have facilities, although not immediately in the courtroom, and they could have made use of them. I mean, what I am appealing for, as a Trial Chamber, is more flexibility. It's not a question of cooperation. I understand that sometimes the way these problems arise are more or less thrown upon us, and the solution is not always easy. And we are only talking of two days in any case. But had you given -- or after consulting your two partners, your two colleagues, identified at least on a prima facie basis that these were documents that you were going to face the witness with eventually, you could have come forward with the -- in a more flexible manner and I'm sure that Ms. Korner wouldn't have said no to receiving the three documents in B/C/S and then look into the matter further within the possibilities of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand, Your Honour, and you're right. I'll try in the future to have the documents carefully reviewed before I send them to the translator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of three pages; we are not talking of three volumes. If you had received a voluminous amount of documentation, which I can't expect your colleagues to translate while they are supposed to be here in the courtroom with you, I would have been more comprehending.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I receive very many documents from Banja Luka, Your Honour, and I can tell you a great number of them are totally irrelevant to what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My suggestion is to resort to a more flexible approach, which would spare us having to waste time on aggravations that are aggravations. I mean, I must concede that they are very legitimate ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will do the best I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other matter, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me see what Ms. Korner says about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We had reserved this for the issue of the journalist and I thought I was going to get to talk about that and we have used up the whole time on something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate that and I know that but the difficulty is, I'm afraid that Mr. Ackerman seems to have forgotten that the reference to the documents that arrived from Banja Luka was not in relation to this witness but to another witness sometime ago. So these documents cannot have arrived on the 26th, which is the day before yesterday -- or the first he heard of it. Your Honour, the other matter is and I'm trying to find it, this issue of Muslims and Croats being prosecuted but not Serbs, wasn't something that was said for the first time the other day. I'm trying to find the passage in one of the statements, but Your Honour, all that I'm saying at the moment is that this question of taking the Prosecution by surprise, which is in our submission what is really all about, it doesn't assist matters because all it does is ends up with an argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with that you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Like this. So for the moment, Your Honour, I maintain, however, my objection to the admissibility of these documents until I'm told, as we were obliged to do with the Prosecution documents, the source from which they were obtained and, secondly, whether or not there are any documents that show the outcome of any proceedings that were taken in relation to these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. I take it the first point is important. In other words, be prepared the earliest opportunity that you have or is convenient to you to bring forward evidence as to the origin or at least make a statement as to the origin of these documents. The rest, I think, I cannot concede to you, Ms. Korner, because it's a matter that can be -- can form part of the evidence that the Defence will be bringing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. later on, and we can visit that later on. However, with regard to the admission of the documents, on the prima facie basis of indicia of reliability, I think we have to apply the same standard, once it has been contested by the Prosecution, I think it has to be taken in hand by you, Mr. Ackerman, and provide the Tribunal with a prima facie indication as to the origin of these documents, even though they are stamped and signed. I mean, what is important is to tell us how the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like me to bring the investigator from Banja Luka to testify about that source?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to tell you what I would like or what I wouldn't like. As it is, you know that hearsay, the hearsay rule here is not applied here as it is applied in your country or in my country or in Ms. Korner's country. If you have the information, you can make an official statement tomorrow morning and then it's up to the Tribunal to decide whether that is in itself a sufficient indicia of reliability and we move forward from there. With regard to the outcome of these documents, we will -- that's your problem later on. But I think I have made myself understood. Before we conclude, I think I ought to invite you to just tell me in a few words what your submission with regard to newspaper reports is, very briefly, not going to be discussed now, but at least we will go home prepared knowing what it is all about and tomorrow morning then we can thrash it out first thing before we continue with the evidence of Mr. Dzonlic. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. There are two newspaper reports. They are dated March of 1993, significantly beyond the scope of the indictment. They refer to statements allegedly made by Mr. Brdjanin in March of 1993. It's the Prosecution's contention with regard to his statements, as I understand it, that they are important for the effect they had on what happened during the course of the indictment and anything he said after that period, it seems to me, could not have affected before that period and therefore I think they are simply irrelevant and not admissible. And now, if the Court decides otherwise, then we have to deal with some additional issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, please make sure that I have a printout of this last statement by Mr. Ackerman so that I will have it before me tomorrow morning when we discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, can I say that the reason we seek to put this in is not to show the effect that it would have had on the people of Banja Luka but to show the state of mind of Mr. Brdjanin with the going to his direct intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The whole -- the printout would also include what Ms. Korner has just stated. I thank you. My apologies to the interpreters. We have overstepped the limits by about two minutes. I promise I will not do it again, if I can help it. I thank you all. We will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: reconvened on Friday the 1st day of March, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
